assign.request: Soften the 100-line file rule to a try; add parts-as-classes and the static-nested Subclassing pattern (List.View / Sortable.List.View / new this.constructor.Thing) to the code skill.
steps: Read the code skill, confirm the 100-line wording
Soften 100 lines to a try, with the split-only-when-logical caveat
Write parts-as-classes: if a class needs several things, give the thing a class
Write Subclassing: static nesting, inheritance through extends, override per branch
Name this.constructor.Thing as the dynamic lookup
Name the file-sprawl diagnosis the 100-line rule caused
Verify the skill still scans tight

assign.outcome:
**The `code` skill now teaches subclassing** — a new §3, and the 100-line rule is a *try*.

- **§3 Parts are classes — hang them on the constructor.** If a class needs several things, give the thing a class; more classes, not more files. Parts attach as statics, so `extends` carries the whole machine down the chain (`Sortable.List.View === List.View` with nothing wired); reassigning one replaces it for that branch only; `new this.constructor.View(…)` resolves per branch at runtime where `new List.View(…)` would hard-code the base. Verified in node — inheritance, override, base untouched, dynamic dispatch all hold.
- **§8** — *try* to keep a file under ~100 lines: a signal to look, not a rule. Past it, ask whether a logical piece wants its own class; split only when the seam is real, and 500 lines that belong together are fine. Names the diagnosis: the old hard 100 is why modules here carry 5–20 sub-files where another class in the same file was the answer.
- Frontmatter description updated so the skill announces the pattern.

**Left deliberately:** no existing module was restructured — this is the convention, not a refactor. The 5–20-sub-file modules stay as they are until something touches them.
